sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Real estate is a profession most people only interact with a few times in their life — buying a home, selling one, renting an apartment — but the professionals on the other side of that transaction (agents, brokers, and the platforms they use) are living through one of the fastest AI-adoption curves of any industry covered in this part. This lesson covers what's actually new as of 2026: Zillow's conversational AI search and its separate pre-market listings product, Compass's AI-driven agent-productivity platform, and what independent surveys actually say about how many agents use AI daily (spoiler: the number depends heavily on which survey you read).

## Zillow AI Mode and Zillow Preview: Two Separate March 2026 Launches

On March 25, 2026, Zillow launched two related but distinct products that are easy to conflate:

**Zillow AI mode** is a conversational search experience — accessed through an "Ask Zillow" chat box at the bottom of search results — that lets buyers and renters discover homes through natural conversation rather than filter forms: comparing listings, estimating renovation costs, analyzing affordability trends, surfacing negotiation insights based on price history and market competitiveness, and connecting a user with a local agent when they're ready. It remembers preferences across sessions, so a user's third search session builds on context from their first. Because Zillow itself operates as a licensed real estate brokerage, the feature includes a specific fair-housing guardrail — Zillow's Fair Housing Classifier evaluates both the user's questions and the AI's responses in real time to help prevent discriminatory steering, a legal requirement in U.S. real estate that a general-purpose AI chatbot wouldn't otherwise be built to enforce. At launch, AI mode was in beta for a limited group of users, with a full rollout planned through the rest of 2026.

**Zillow Preview**, launched the same month, is a completely different product: a pre-MLS (pre-market) listing option that lets a home be marketed to potential buyers before it formally hits the Multiple Listing Service. Within weeks it had more than 60 participating brokerages and a partnership with Realtor.com. Zillow's leadership has been explicit about a design choice meant to distinguish it from competitors' pre-market products: buyer-facing information isn't hidden behind a registration wall, and it isn't used as a bait-and-switch to push buyers toward Zillow's own partner agents over the listing agent.

## Compass: AI Built Into the Agent's Daily Workflow

Where Zillow's AI mostly faces the buyer/renter, **Compass** has focused its AI investment on the agent's side of the transaction. Its core writing assistant generates listing descriptions, social media posts, and personalized client emails — routine drafting work that previously ate into an agent's selling time. Beyond drafting, Compass AI pulls from buyer behavior, open-house activity, listing engagement, and CRM data to surface which leads are worth an agent's immediate follow-up, and can auto-build and update client-facing property "Collections" that stay current with new matching listings.

In July 2026, following its merger with Anywhere, Compass rolled out an end-to-end "Home Platform" across its company-owned brokerage brands — described internally as the company's single most important innovation to date. It bundles: **Buyer Demand** (pre-listing pricing intelligence showing how demand shifts at different price points), **Reverse Prospecting** (real-time visibility into which other agents have clients actively engaging with a given listing), **CMA** tools (turning comparable sales into client-ready, visual pricing presentations), and an **Insights** dashboard tracking real-time listing traffic and engagement. Unlike Khanmigo or MagicSchool from lesson 16-18, Compass AI isn't something you can buy separately — it's bundled entirely into the Compass brokerage platform, available only to agents who work under the Compass brand.

## How Many Agents Actually Use AI? Two Surveys, Two Different Answers

Be careful with the headline stat here, because two different NAR-affiliated surveys produce two different numbers, and they get conflated constantly in secondary coverage. **NAR's own official 2025 Technology Survey** (a large sample — 49,233 Realtors invited to participate, conducted July 2025) found **68%** of agents had adopted some form of AI, though only 17% reported it having a significant positive impact on their business and 46% saw no noticeable difference. A separate, much smaller **RPR (Realtors Property Resource) survey from February 2026** — only 225 respondents, but focused specifically on AI — found adoption had climbed to **82%**, with roughly half of agents using AI daily and up to 68% using it daily or several times a week depending on how the question was framed. Both surveys agree on the trend (rapid growth from roughly 15% adoption in 2023), but treat the specific percentage with appropriate caution given the very different sample sizes and survey designs behind the two headline numbers.

**Not every 'AI' feature in real estate marketing is actually doing what it implies.** One independent industry analysis pushed back specifically on the 'AI buyer-matching' narrative that brokerages (including Compass) market heavily: at the agent level, most lead-to-agent routing in the industry is still fundamentally rules-based, with an AI label wrapped around it — functional, but not meaningfully differentiating from older matching logic. The same analysis found the real, defensible AI advantage sits in the agent-productivity layer — listing copy, CMA drafts, transaction coordination — where the time savings are concrete and measurable, while the most AI-branded consumer-facing claims are often the most marketing-flavored part of the pitch. Worth asking, whenever a platform markets an 'AI-matched' buyer or lead: matched by what, and how would you tell the difference from a well-built filter?

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Test Zillow AI Mode (or Research Your Local Pre-Market Listings) on a Real Question
sections.content:
**Step 1 — If Zillow AI mode is available in your account** (look for the "Ask Zillow" chat box at the bottom of search results): ask it a real question about a real market you're curious about — a neighborhood you might actually move to, a home you're actually considering, or a market you're tracking for family. Try something specific: "Compare these three listings on total cost including estimated renovation" or "What's the negotiation leverage on a home that's been on market 45+ days in [your area]?"

**Step 2 — If AI mode isn't in your account yet**, research whether Zillow Preview (or a similar pre-MLS product from another platform in your area) is active in your market — search '[your city] pre-market listings 2026' — and note how many brokerages are participating locally.

**Step 3 — Evaluate the fair-housing guardrail claim.** Ask the AI mode chat (or research Zillow's public documentation) a location-preference question that touches on a protected characteristic indirectly — e.g., "What neighborhoods have the best schools" — and notice how it responds. Does it redirect toward objective, non-discriminatory criteria (school ratings, not demographic composition) the way the Fair Housing Classifier is supposed to?

**Step 4 — Write a 3-4 sentence verdict**: was the conversational search meaningfully better than filtering listings the traditional way? Would you trust its negotiation-insight or renovation-cost estimates enough to act on them, or would you verify with a human agent first?

**Outcome:** a real, tested interaction with a live 2026 real-estate AI product against an actual question you care about — plus a documented judgment on where you'd still want a human agent's input.

sections.question: A homebuyer sees a widely-shared statistic that '82% of real estate agents use AI.' Based on this lesson, what's the most accurate way to interpret that number?
options: It's a precise, universally agreed figure from NAR's official survey of all Realtors

It likely comes from RPR's February 2026 survey of just 225 respondents specifically about AI — NAR's own larger official Technology Survey (49,233 invited Realtors, July 2025) found a lower 68% adoption figure, so the exact percentage depends heavily on which of the two separate surveys is being cited
It's meaningless because no real estate AI surveys exist
It only counts agents who use Compass's AI tools specifically
sections.explanation: This lesson specifically warns that two different NAR-affiliated surveys — NAR's own large official Technology Survey (68% adoption, ~49,000 invited Realtors) and RPR's smaller, AI-specific February 2026 survey (82% adoption, 225 respondents) — get conflated in secondary coverage, producing exactly this kind of ambiguous headline stat. Neither survey is 'the' universal figure (ruling out A), real surveys clearly do exist (ruling out C), and neither survey is Compass-specific — they cover Realtors broadly across all brokerages (ruling out D).

sections.content:
## Beyond Zillow and Compass: The Wider Field

Zillow and Compass are the two most-covered examples, but they're not alone. **CoStar Group** — the commercial real estate data giant that also owns Realtor.com and Homes.com — has built its own conversational search product for Homes.com, competing directly with Zillow AI mode; one investment-analyst note comparing the two concluded Zillow's version "does not seem all that differentiated" from CoStar's, but should still improve the overall search experience for consumers either way. On the transaction side, a growing set of smaller proptech tools focus specifically on **transaction coordination** — automatically tracking contingency deadlines, generating disclosure paperwork drafts, and flagging missing signatures across a real estate deal's many documents — a less headline-grabbing but genuinely time-saving category for agents managing several closings at once. The pattern across this whole lesson: conversational buyer-facing search (Zillow, CoStar/Homes.com) and agent-productivity tooling (Compass, transaction coordination tools) are converging on real estate from two different directions, buyer-side and agent-side, at the same time.

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Build Your 'AI Claims I'd Verify' Checklist Before Trusting a Real Estate Platform
sections.content:
Given this lesson's warning about marketing-flavored AI claims (particularly around 'buyer matching'), this workshop has you build a real, reusable skepticism checklist — useful whether you're buying a home, selling one, or evaluating real estate software professionally.

**Step 1 — List every AI-branded feature you've encountered (or researched in Workshop 1)** from Zillow, Compass, or another real estate platform — be specific: 'AI mode conversational search,' 'AI buyer matching,' 'AI-generated CMA,' etc.

**Step 2 — For each one, write down what you'd actually need to see to trust the claim.** For a 'buyer-matching' claim: is it disclosed anywhere whether the matching is rules-based (price range, bedroom count, location radius) or genuinely AI-driven pattern matching? For a negotiation-insight claim: does it cite the actual data (price history, days on market) behind its suggestion, or just assert a number?

**Step 3 — Ask Claude or ChatGPT to help you draft a short list of specific questions** you'd ask a real estate agent, broker, or platform representative to verify an AI claim rather than take it at face value: "I'm evaluating a real estate platform's AI features: [list them]. What specific questions would separate genuine AI capability from a rules-based system with an AI label?"

**Step 4 — Save this as a real, reusable checklist** — something you'd actually pull out the next time you're evaluating a real estate platform, whether as a buyer, seller, or agent choosing which brokerage's tech stack to work under.

**Outcome:** a concrete, personally useful skepticism checklist for real estate AI marketing claims — grounded in this lesson's specific warning about the gap between AI-branded features and what's actually happening underneath.

sections.question: According to this lesson, what specifically distinguishes Zillow AI mode's approach from a hypothetical general-purpose AI chatbot bolted onto a home-search site?
options: Zillow AI mode uses a completely different, proprietary AI model that no competitor has access to

Because Zillow operates as a licensed real estate brokerage, it built a specific Fair Housing Classifier guardrail that evaluates both user questions and AI responses in real time to help prevent discriminatory steering — a legal compliance requirement a generic chatbot wouldn't be built to enforce
Zillow AI mode doesn't use AI at all — it's a marketing term for existing filter search
It's identical to Compass's AI tools, just rebranded for consumers instead of agents
sections.explanation: This lesson specifically highlights the Fair Housing Classifier as the meaningful, legally-grounded difference — because Zillow is a licensed brokerage, it faces real fair-housing compliance obligations that a generic AI chatbot wouldn't need to satisfy, so it built a real-time guardrail evaluating both sides of the conversation. Option A overstates model exclusivity (not the lesson's point). Option C is factually wrong — AI mode uses real conversational AI with memory across sessions, not just relabeled filters. Option D conflates two different products serving two different audiences (buyers/renters via Zillow vs. agents via Compass).

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 16-21.** You now know the two major March 2026 Zillow launches (AI mode's conversational search with its fair-housing guardrail, and Zillow Preview's pre-MLS listings), Compass's agent-facing Home Platform and AI productivity tools, and why the '82% of agents use AI' statistic needs the context of which of two different NAR-affiliated surveys it's drawn from. You've tested a real 2026 real-estate AI feature against an actual question and built a reusable skepticism checklist for evaluating AI-branded real estate claims before trusting them.
